body_paragraphs: The war just widened. Sirens sounded across Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar before dawn Friday as Iran's Revolutionary Guard launched fresh drone strikes and the US carried out its 13th straight night of strikes on Iran. Iran rejected an Iraqi-mediated ceasefire outright, and Trump told Axios he's weighing a 'massive attack, bigger than ever before.' Brent, which broke $100 a barrel Thursday for the first time since May, eased only slightly Friday morning. Stocks already took the hit: the S&P fell 1.21%, the Nasdaq 2.15% - Tesla down 14.5% on an earnings miss, Alphabet down 7% on ballooning AI capex - and the 10-year hit its highest yield since January 2025. FOMC hike odds have more than doubled since Wednesday, to roughly 36%.

Locally, the Heat's accidental leak looks less accidental by the day: the team confirmed the LeBron press-conference page was real prep, just published early, and Kalshi now has Miami's odds at 51%, up from 39% - though Rich Paul says there's still no timetable. The Marlins get their first game back tonight since the nine-game skid, hosting the Padres with the wild-card cushion long gone.

Beyond the feed: this week marks roughly a century since the hurricane that leveled Miami Beach and, almost by accident, gave it the Art Deco identity it's known for now - proof some of a city's best features were never the plan. A Stoic newsletter worth your Sunday argues a good day doesn't have to be earned by getting everything right.

Iran rejected an Iraqi-mediated ceasefire proposal outright. Trump told Axios he's 'considering a massive attack, bigger than ever before' and is 'close to making a decision.' themes.title: A hurricane, a rebuild, and a century of Art Deco
themes.thesis: Miami Beach's most recognizable identity was never the plan - it was what got built after the plan got destroyed.
themes.synthesis: The Great Miami Hurricane of 1926 leveled much of Miami Beach; the pastel, geometric Art Deco buildings that came to define the neighborhood didn't start appearing until the 1930s, designed by architects like Henry Hohauser borrowing forms from ocean liners and machines. Barbara Capitman and a group of friends founded the Miami Design Preservation League in 1976 to save those same buildings from demolition when they were considered too new to matter; the district made the National Register in 1979, the first 20th-century historic district in the country.
themes.new_today: Outside the feed: a century since the storm that forced the rebuild, and a half-century since the League that saved what got built.
themes.why_it_matters: A useful corrective on a week that's mostly been about oil and odds - the thing everyone now recognizes as Miami Beach's identity was almost torn down twice, once by a hurricane and once by neglect.

themes.title: A good day doesn't have to be earned
themes.thesis: The Stoic case against needing to deserve an ordinary day.
themes.synthesis: This week's Sunday Snippets from What Is Stoicism? argues for lowering the threshold on what counts as a good day - not one earned through productivity, discipline, or getting everything right, but simply one where you woke up, which is itself a gift not everyone gets. A companion piece the same week argues that asking for help isn't weakness, and that vulnerability is what deepens friendship rather than threatening it.
themes.new_today: New this week: both pieces, arguing the same point from different angles.
themes.why_it_matters: Directly adjacent to what you wrote this month about guilt and providing - worth reading as description of what's already true, not another instruction to do more.

rabbit_hole.title: Uncovering a Global Ancient History Beyond Greece and Rome
rabbit_hole.creator: Carlos Noreña, Aeon
rabbit_hole.why: Noreña, a Berkeley historian, argues the 'ancient world' most of us were taught is a fraction of the real one - the Indian Ocean, not the Mediterranean, was the actual geographic core of premodern Afro-Eurasia. It's the kind of reframe that changes how you read everything else this week without asking anything of you in return.

beautiful_thing.title: The Colony Hotel
beautiful_thing.creator: Henry Hohauser, architect
beautiful_thing.body: At 736 Ocean Drive, the Colony Hotel is considered the first fully streamlined building on Ocean Drive, its plans completed in July 1935 by Henry Hohauser, one of the earliest architects to bring that style to Miami Beach. The symmetrical facade is built around an inverted-T marquee bearing the hotel's name, with banded teal stripes separating three floors of glass block windows and horizontal eyebrows shading them from the sun; the sign's black lettering on lilac neon is one of the most photographed in the district. The hotel opened with fifty rooms, each with a private bathroom, a detail unusual enough at the time to be worth advertising.

daily_puzzle.prompt: A father is now three times as old as his son. In 12 years, he'll only be twice as old. How old is the son right now?
daily_puzzle.hint: Set up two equations - one for 'now,' one for '12 years from now' - and let the son's current age be the unknown.
daily_puzzle.explanation: If the son is s, the father is 3s now. In 12 years: 3s + 12 = 2(s + 12), which simplifies to s = 12 - so the son is 12 and the father is 36.
